content: 1. The protective efficacy of the vaccine becomes evident 10 days after the administration of the second dose, with an approximate cost of $40 per dose. Studies have demonstrated an overall protective efficacy of 85–90%, lasting for at least six months across all age groups. However, in children under five years of age, the efficacy declines rapidly after this period. 2. A second vaccine, which contains both O1 and O139 Vibrio cholerae serotypes but lacks the recombinant B subunit, has been developed and used exclusively in Vietnam. More recently, this vaccine has been reformulated under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) conditions by the International Vaccine Institute and submitted to the World Health Organization (WHO) for prequalification. It has also been licensed in India under the name Shanchol by Shanta Biotech and is marketed at approximately $6 per dose. This vaccine has shown longer-term protection in children under five years of age, although it appears to be less protective than Dukoral. 3. The use of these vaccines in endemic areas, as well as their preemptive use during periods of high epidemic risk, has been recommended. In cholera-endemic countries, vaccination should be considered an additional tool for controlling cholera, targeting high-risk populations. 4. Vaccine development for shigellosis has been challenging, as the most effective vaccines are also the most reactogenic. Consequently, no Shigella vaccine candidate has been seriously considered for large-scale implementation. This is partly due to the multiple species and serotypes of Shigella capable of causing human illness. Additionally, while immunity is known to be serotype-specific, the exact nature of the protective immunity required for an effective vaccine remains unclear. 5. Various approaches to Shigella vaccine development have been explored, including oral immunization with live attenuated Shigella or Salmonella typhi expressing Shigella O-antigens, isolated Shigella cell-surface components, and parenterally administered O-polysaccharide-protein conjugates. A pentavalent vaccine targeting Shigella dysenteriae type 1, Shigella sonnei, and three Shigella flexneri serotypes (2a, 3a, and 6) has been proposed to provide broad protection against most Shigella species and serotypes. However, the development of such a vaccine remains a formidable task. 6. Targeting animal reservoirs has been a strategy to reduce the transmission of zoonotic diseases to humans. For example, chemotherapy has been used to reduce the animal reservoir of human sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma rhodesiense in Uganda. However, culling domestic dogs in response to rabies outbreaks has not shown significant effects on rabies control. Similarly, culling wildlife has not provided a long-term solution for controlling wildlife rabies due to factors such as high reproductive potential, movement patterns, and environmental conditions. 7. Empirical evidence suggests that mass vaccination of reservoir hosts, whether domestic dogs or wildlife, remains the most effective approach to rabies control and elimination. Examples include the use of vaccines in dogs for rabies control and the distribution of baited oral vaccines for fox populations in Europe. 8. The development of a vaccine for bovines to control Schistosoma japonicum is under consideration in China and the Philippines, depending on the proportion of human cases derived from buffalo sources. The effectiveness of such vaccines will depend on the proportion of infections in other reservoir hosts that cannot be vaccinated. 9. For echinococcosis and cysticercosis, targeting major animal reservoirs such as sheep and pigs has been investigated. Ovine vaccines have been tested for echinococcosis, while oxfenbendazole has been used to kill larval cysts in pigs, the source of human tapeworm infections. However, these approaches often require additional interventions to reinforce their impact, necessitating integrated strategies. 10. Infectious diseases, particularly neglected diseases, thrive in conditions of poverty, inadequate sanitation, and lack of formal education. These diseases perpetuate poverty, limiting opportunities for development and education. Education is strongly associated with better health outcomes, such as reduced infant, child, and maternal mortality rates, and is a key strategy for ending poverty and reducing the burden of disease. 11. The WHO has identified literacy as a key determinant for reducing health inequities. Studies have shown that higher levels of education are associated with lower exposure to infectious diseases. For example, in Honduras, Taenia solium infections are more prevalent among individuals with fewer years of schooling. In rural Peru, lack of education beyond elementary school is associated with higher levels of T. solium seropositivity. 12. While education and awareness are assumed to lead to behavior change, the relationship between knowledge and action is not always straightforward. For instance, in Sri Lanka, despite awareness of rabies, there was no improvement in responsible dog ownership. Similarly, in Mozambique, knowledge about porcine cysticercosis did not reduce its prevalence among households. 13. The effectiveness of health education interventions often depends on the context and the involvement of the community. Long-term studies and participatory research are needed to optimize educational strategies. For example, a 12-year pilot study in China focusing on health education and treatment for Schistosoma japonicum achieved long-term positive changes, particularly among women. 14. The PRECEDE-PROCEED model, widely used in health promotion, provides a comprehensive framework for assessing needs and implementing interventions. It emphasizes multidimensional, multisectoral, and participatory efforts to address health risks. However, it requires significant professional involvement and an organized system. 15. Outcome Mapping is another approach that engages stakeholders to define desired outcomes, implement strategies, and measure progress. Unlike the PRECEDE-PROCEED model, Outcome Mapping allows for real-time assessment of progress and behavioral changes. 16. Health literacy is fundamental in empowering individuals and communities to take actions that improve their health and environment. While health literacy has been shown to foster positive health behaviors for chronic disease prevention, its role in addressing infectious diseases in impoverished communities remains underexplored. 17. Addressing zoonotic diseases often requires integrated strategies that go beyond education and awareness. For example, controlling Schistosoma japonicum in China involves addressing agricultural practices and the role of water buffalo as a reservoir. Strategies such as replacing or treating water buffalo and using transmission-blocking vaccines are necessary to maximize control efforts. 18. Discrepancies between knowledge and action in reducing zoonotic disease burdens may be influenced by economic incentives, health risk perceptions, and environmental conditions. For instance, small-scale pig holders may lack the resources to confine their animals, despite understanding the risks of cysticercosis. 19. The effectiveness of health education interventions in endemic communities may also reflect the need for longer-term studies, optimized educational designs, and innovative evaluation methods. Community participation is crucial for achieving lasting effects, as demonstrated in Nepal and Tanzania, where participatory approaches led to significant behavioral changes and reduced disease incidence.
